Gateway plus BFF plus internal gRPC Public traffic enters through a gateway that handles auth and rate limits, hits a client-specific BFF, which calls internal services over gRPC. Nothing internal is reachable from outside. Event stream plus CDC plus lakehouse Operational events flow through a stream; CDC captures the database changes that predate the event design; both land in the lakehouse for analytics. The lakehouse never feeds an operational decision back synchronously. Queue plus saga for long-running business processes An order, a claim, a loan application: a saga orchestrator steps through services via queues, each step idempotent, each with a compensating action, with the state of every in-flight process visible in one place. Strangler with an anti-corruption layer New services sit behind the same gateway as the legacy system; an anti-corruption layer translates between the legacy model and the new domain model so the new services never inherit the old shape. See Legacy Modernization Execution . Governance The rules an architecture review should enforce Pattern choice is a team decision. These rules are the small set an Architecture Review Board should hold across teams, because violating them is expensive for everyone else. Every published contract (OpenAPI, proto, event schema) is versioned, in a repository, reviewed, and never broken in place No service reads another service's database; the only path is the contract Every asynchronous consumer is idempotent and has a dead-letter path with an owner Every synchronous call across a network boundary has a timeout, a retry policy with backoff, and a circuit breaker Every integration is observable end to end: a correlation identifier propagates through calls and messages, and a trace exists for a single business transaction Domain events describe business facts in business language, not table changes Internal integration does not go through a vendor iPaaS unless the vendor owns both ends; iPaaS is for SaaS-to-SaaS Any integration that runs on a schedule has an alert when it does not run, not only when it fails Common pitfall The enterprise service bus reborn as a platform Every decade the same mistake arrives under a new name: a central integration team owning a central integration product through which everything must pass. What it looks like The integration team owns the bus, the iPaaS, or the event platform, and every new integration is a ticket to that team. Transformations accumulate inside the product where no product team can see them. The team becomes the bottleneck for every delivery, the product becomes the system nobody dares upgrade, and the business logic that leaked into it is the next modernization project. The counter-move A central team owns the platform (the broker, the gateway, the schema registry, the observability) and the rules above. Product teams own their contracts, their consumers, their transformations, and their on-call. The platform team's success metric is how little any team needs to talk to them. See Platform Engineering for the operating model.

title: Technical Debt Economics
description: Turning technical debt into three numbers per item (carry cost, risk exposure, remediation cost), a browser calculator that ranks a debt portfolio by return on the remediation dollar and sequences it across years within a budget, where high-ratio debt hides, and the debt-budget pitfall that funds nothing in particular.
body: Technical Debt Economics Framework Three numbers per item, or it is not a debt conversation Technical debt discussions fail because they are conducted in adjectives. An item is not fundable until it has a carry cost, a remediation cost, and a risk exposure, each stated in dollars per year. Rough is fine. Absent is not. Number What it is How to estimate it in an hour Carry cost What the debt costs every year it stays: slower delivery, extra operational toil, licensing for the thing you should have retired, the workaround everyone maintains Engineering hours per month spent working around it, times a loaded hourly rate, times twelve, plus any hard costs (licenses, hosting, support contracts) that exist only because of it Risk exposure The expected annual cost of the incident, breach, or outage the debt makes more likely Probability of a material event in a year, times the cost of that event (revenue, recovery, credits, regulatory). A 20 percent chance of a $500k event is $100k a year. Precision is not the point; the order of magnitude is Remediation cost What it costs to make it go away, once Engineering hours to fix, migrate, or retire, times the loaded rate, plus any one-time hard costs. Include the cost of the parallel run or cutover if there is one Carry cost plus risk exposure is the annual cost of doing nothing. Divided into remediation cost it gives the payback period. Items with a payback under a year are not debt decisions; they are operating decisions that have been avoided. Items with a payback over five years are usually not worth doing unless the risk exposure is dominated by a tail event that the organization has said it will not accept, which is what Technology Risk Appetite is for. Interactive Carry-cost calculator and multi-year sequencer Enter up to eight debt items and an annual remediation budget. The tool computes annual cost of doing nothing, payback, and a ranking, then sequences the items across years within the budget. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Loaded engineering cost per hour ($) Annual remediation budget ($) Planning horizon (years) Item Hours / month lost to it Hard carry cost / yr ($) Event probability / yr (%) Event cost ($) Remediation hours Remediation hard cost ($) Rank and sequence Load sample portfolio Clear Method How the sequencer decides The logic is deliberately simple enough to explain to a CFO in one sentence: fund the items that remove the most annual cost per remediation dollar, within the budget, and carry the rest. Annual cost of doing nothing Carry cost plus risk exposure, for each item. Ratio Annual cost of doing nothing divided by remediation cost. This is the return on the remediation dollar. Items are ranked by it. Greedy allocation by year Walk the ranked list. If an item fits in the current year's remaining budget, fund it that year. If it does not fit, carry it to the next year and keep walking so smaller items can use the remaining capacity. Repeat for the horizon. Carry cost paid meanwhile Every year an item is not yet remediated, its annual cost of doing nothing is paid. The total across the horizon is reported so the sequence can be compared against a different budget. What it does not do It does not model dependencies between items, capacity constraints per team, or the option of partial remediation. The private version does; this is the transparent core. A sequencing decision that cannot be explained is one the CFO will not fund twice. Worked example Reading a ranked portfolio Load the sample portfolio above. The ranking usually surprises people in the same way. What the ranking shows The item everyone talks about, the large monolith rewrite, ranks low: a large remediation cost against a carry cost that is real but diffuse. The item nobody talks about, an unsupported database version with a meaningful breach probability, ranks first because its risk exposure dominates and its remediation is cheap. A small integration workaround that costs one engineer a week a month ranks second. Two of the top four items cost less than $50k to fix. What to do with it Fund the top of the list this quarter without a further business case; the numbers are the case. Take the monolith to the capital allocation conversation as a transform investment, not a debt item, because that is what it is. Report the annual cost of doing nothing for the unfunded remainder to the board as a number, once a year, so nobody can later say the risk was hidden. Reference Where debt hides and how to find it The backlog in Application Portfolio Management and the signals in Technology Diligence are the inputs. These are the places that reliably produce items with high ratios. Source What to look for Typical carry cost driver Unsupported or end-of-life versions Runtimes, databases, operating systems, and frameworks past vendor support Risk exposure; also extended support contracts and the inability to patch Manual operational toil Deployments, restores, certificate renewals, and data fixes done by hand Hours per month, plus the outage each one eventually causes Duplicated capability Two or more systems doing the same job because a migration stopped halfway Double licensing, double integration, double on-call Undocumented single-person systems Anything only one engineer can change Key-person risk expressed as a probability times the cost of losing them Missing tests on critical paths Change failure rate concentrated in a few services Incident cost and the slowdown of every change to those services Deferred security findings Pen test and scan findings older than one quarter Almost pure risk exposure; usually cheap to remediate relative to it Workarounds in the integration layer Transformations and retries that exist because a contract was never fixed Hours per month and the incidents when the workaround meets an edge case Common pitfall The debt budget that funds nothing in particular Allocating twenty percent of capacity to debt without a ranked list produces twenty percent of capacity spent on whatever each team finds annoying. What it looks like Every sprint has a debt allocation. Engineers use it to refactor code they touch anyway. The unsupported database, which nobody enjoys working on, is untouched for three years. The allocation is visible in the roadmap, so leadership believes debt is being managed. The breach, when it comes, is on the database. The counter-move The debt allocation funds the ranked list, top down, and nothing else. Local refactoring is part of normal delivery, not the debt budget. The list is reviewed quarterly, new items need the three numbers to get on it, and the annual cost of doing nothing for the unfunded tail is reported alongside the items funded. See Engineering Metrics for the delivery signals that tell you whether the carry cost estimates were right.

title: Identity & Access Architecture
description: The identity layer as a control plane: workforce, privileged, workload, and customer populations, a reference architecture mapped across Entra, AWS, Google Cloud, and independent platforms, joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle, non-human and agent identity, sequencing by risk reduced, and the one export that reveals how seriously identity has been taken.
body: Identity & Access Architecture Framework Identity is the control plane, not a service Every other security control assumes the request came from who it says it did. If that assumption is weak, segmentation, detection, and encryption are all decorating an open door. Most estates have at least four identity populations, and most identity programs are built for only the first. The others are where the breaches happen. Population What it covers Where it usually is Where it needs to be Workforce Employees and contractors signing in to SaaS, VPN, and internal apps SSO for the big apps, local accounts for everything else, MFA on the VPN only One directory, every app federated, phishing-resistant MFA everywhere, no local accounts left standing Privileged Admins of cloud tenants, directories, databases, network, and the identity platform itself Standing global admin held by six people, shared break-glass account in a password manager No standing privilege. Just-in-time elevation with approval, time-bound, logged, and reviewed. Break-glass accounts monitored, tested quarterly Workload Service principals, managed identities, IAM roles, API keys, CI runners, agents Long-lived secrets in config, keys created by whoever needed one, nobody knows how many exist Managed identities or short-lived federated tokens wherever the platform supports them, secrets in a vault with rotation, an inventory with owners Customer and partner External users of your products and B2B partners reaching internal systems Built into each product separately, partner access through a shared VPN account A dedicated customer identity platform with its own risk policy, partners federated to their own directory with scoped, expiring access Reference architecture The layers a mature identity estate has Provider names differ; the structure does not. The table maps each layer to what it looks like on the major platforms so an architecture review can ask whether each layer exists, not which product it uses. Layer Purpose Microsoft Entra AWS Google Cloud Independent Authoritative source One system of record for who exists, in what role, reporting to whom HR system feeding Entra ID via provisioning HR system feeding IAM Identity Center via an external IdP HR system feeding Cloud Identity via an external IdP Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, or similar as source; Okta or Entra as the directory Directory and federation Single identity, federated to every application Entra ID with SAML and OIDC apps, Enterprise Apps gallery IAM Identity Center for AWS accounts, external IdP for everything else Cloud Identity plus an external IdP Okta, Ping Authentication policy Decide per request whether to allow, step up, or block, based on risk Conditional Access with sign-in and user risk from Identity Protection IdP-side policy; AWS does not own workforce authentication policy IdP-side policy; Context-Aware Access for Google resources Okta Adaptive MFA, Ping policy engine Privileged access Time-bound elevation with approval and audit Privileged Identity Management for roles and groups, Administrative Units for scope Permission sets in IAM Identity Center with short session durations; no standing admin in the management account IAM Conditions with time bounds, Privileged Access Manager CyberArk, BeyondTrust, or the IdP's own JIT feature Workload identity Services authenticate without long-lived secrets Managed identities, workload identity federation for GitHub and Kubernetes IAM roles, IRSA and Pod Identity for EKS, OIDC federation for CI Service accounts with workload identity federation, no downloaded keys SPIFFE and SPIRE for cross-platform workloads Secrets The credentials that cannot be eliminated, held once, rotated, audited Key Vault Secrets Manager, Parameter Store Secret Manager HashiCorp Vault Governance Access reviews, entitlement packages, separation of duties, certifications Entra ID Governance: access packages, access reviews, lifecycle workflows IAM Access Analyzer for unused access, external IGA for reviews Policy Analyzer, external IGA for reviews SailPoint, Saviynt Device and session Trust the device as well as the user Intune compliance signal into Conditional Access IdP device trust signal Endpoint Verification into Context-Aware Access Jamf, CrowdStrike, or the IdP device trust integration Lifecycle Joiner, mover, leaver: the process that decides whether the architecture works The most sophisticated Conditional Access policy in the world does nothing about the contractor who left eight months ago and still has a working account. Where it fails Access is granted by ticket, on request, by whoever is asked. Nobody removes access when someone changes role, so tenure equals entitlement. Offboarding disables the directory account but not the twelve SaaS apps with local accounts, the shared service credential the person knew, or the API key they created. The access review is an annual spreadsheet that every manager approves in full because rejecting anything means explaining it. What good looks like Birthright access is defined per role and granted automatically from the HR event. Anything beyond birthright is requested through an access package with a named approver and an expiry. A mover event triggers removal of the old role's entitlements, not just addition of the new. A leaver event is a single action that cascades to every federated app within minutes, and there is a report of what could not be cascaded, which is the list of local accounts still to be eliminated. Access reviews are quarterly, scoped to privileged and sensitive entitlements, and the default on no response is removal. Non-human identity The population that is now larger than the workforce In most cloud estates service principals, roles, keys, and automation identities outnumber people three to one and nobody owns the inventory. AI agents are adding to this fast, and they act with whatever identity they are given. The questions to ask, in order: How many exist Pull the full list of service principals, IAM roles, service accounts, and API keys from every cloud tenant and the CI system. If the number is a surprise, that is the finding. Which have an owner Every non-human identity needs a named human owner and a purpose. Anything without one is a candidate for disablement after a quarantine period. Which use long-lived secrets A client secret or access key that does not expire is a credential that will eventually be in a repository, a log, or a former employee's laptop. Migrate to managed identity or federated tokens; where impossible, vault and rotate. Which are over-privileged Most workload identities were granted Contributor or PowerUser because it worked. Use the platform's unused-access analysis to shrink them to what they call. Which can reach production from outside it CI runners and developer tooling that hold production credentials are the standard path from a compromised laptop to a production breach. What identity do agents act with An AI agent that calls tools does so as something. If that something is a broadly-scoped service principal, the agent's judgment is now a security control. Give agents their own scoped identities, short-lived, with the same review cadence as privileged humans. Sequencing Where to start when everything is weak Identity programs fail by trying to do all of this at once and finishing none of it. The order below is by risk reduced per unit of effort. Order Move Why first Evidence it is done 1 Phishing-resistant MFA for all privileged accounts, then everyone Credential theft is the entry point in most breaches; this closes it for the accounts that matter most Sign-in logs show no privileged authentication without FIDO2, passkey, or certificate 2 Eliminate standing privileged access Turns a stolen admin credential from a catastrophe into a logged, time-bound event Zero permanent assignments to global or account-level admin roles; PIM or equivalent activation history exists 3 Federate every application, kill local accounts Offboarding cannot work while apps hold their own passwords Application inventory with a federation status per app and a shrinking count of exceptions 4 Automate joiner, mover, leaver from the HR source Removes the human step that fails, and makes the directory trustworthy as an inventory of people Leaver-to-disabled time measured in minutes; mover events remove old entitlements 5 Inventory and shrink non-human identities The largest and least-governed population An owned inventory, no non-expiring secrets for new identities, a rotation report 6 Risk-based authentication policy and device trust Moves from static rules to per-request decisions Policies in report-only mode first, then enforced, with an exception register 7 Governance: reviews, packages, separation of duties Keeps the estate clean after the cleanup Quarterly review completion with a non-zero removal rate Week one The single artifact that tells you the most For a new CTO, an acquirer, or an auditor, one export answers most of the question of how seriously identity has been taken. What to pull The list of every account holding a privileged role in each cloud tenant and the directory, with whether the assignment is permanent or eligible, when it was last used, and whether the account has phishing-resistant MFA registered. Then the same for service principals with owner-level rights. It takes an hour and requires no tooling beyond what the platform provides. How to read it More than a handful of permanent global admins, any of them shared or belonging to people who have left, any without strong MFA, or any service principal with tenant-wide write access and a non-expiring secret: each is a finding in its own right, and together they say the identity layer has been administered rather than architected. That reading should shape the first quarter's security priorities regardless of what the security roadmap deck says. Common pitfall Buying the identity platform and calling it done Most organizations that fail on identity already own the right products. The failure is in the process, the scope, and the exceptions. MFA is enforced, but the legacy authentication protocols that bypass it are still enabled Conditional Access exists, but the policy has forty exclusions and the exclusion group is the one everyone ends up in PIM is deployed for global admin, but the subscription and resource-group owners are still permanent The HR feed is connected, but contractors are not in HR, so the largest leaver risk is unmanaged Access reviews run, but the approval rate is 100 percent, which means nobody is reviewing The break-glass account exists and has never been tested, or has been tested and used routinely because it is convenient Secrets are in a vault, but the application also has a copy in an environment variable that was never removed

title: Observability & SRE Operating Model
description: How a reliability function is run rather than how much reliability to buy: four operating models and the one most organizations actually run, what the function owns (SLOs, error budget policy, observability standards, alert hygiene, production readiness, toil), an observability architecture that survives scale and cost, an on-call design people will keep doing, a sequence for standing the function up, and the rename-the-ops-team pitfall.
body: Observability & SRE Operating Model Framework Four models, and the one most organizations are actually running Reliability as an Economic Decision answers how much reliability to buy. This page answers how the function that delivers it is organized, because the same reliability budget produces very different outcomes under different operating models. Model Who is on call Who owns reliability work Fits when Fails when Ops team owns production A central operations team The ops team, reactively Small estates, few changes, a product team that cannot be paged Change volume rises; the ops team cannot understand what it is paging on, and the product team has no incentive to build operable software You build it, you run it Each product team, for its own services Each product team Autonomous teams with the platform support to be self-sufficient Teams lack observability tooling, on-call is unfunded, and reliability work loses every prioritization to features Embedded SRE Product team, with an SRE embedded in it Shared; the SRE drives standards and the team executes Critical services that justify a dedicated reliability engineer The SRE becomes the team's ops person and the standards work never happens Central SRE with a platform Product teams for their services; SRE for the platform and for a defined set of critical services SRE owns the platform, the standards, the tooling, and error budget policy; teams own their services within it Ten or more teams and a shared platform, which is most enterprises The SRE team is treated as a rename of the ops team and is paged for everything Most organizations claiming the second model are running the first with extra steps: product teams are nominally on call, but escalate to a central team that does the actual restoration and owns none of the fixes. Naming the model that is actually running is the first honest step. Reference What the function owns An SRE or reliability function that owns only incident response is an operations team. The list below is what distinguishes a reliability function from a rename. Responsibility What it looks like when owned What it looks like when nobody owns it Service level objectives Every customer-facing service has an SLO agreed with its product owner, measured from the user's perspective, reviewed quarterly A 99.9 percent target inherited from a contract, measured at the load balancer, that nobody can explain Error budget policy A written rule for what happens when a service exhausts its budget: feature work pauses, reliability work is prioritized, the product owner signs off The budget is reported and ignored Observability standards A required minimum for any service in production: structured logs, metrics with defined names, traces with propagated correlation, dashboards from a template, alerts tied to SLOs Each team instruments what it thinks of; the incident reveals the gap Alert hygiene Every page maps to a user-visible symptom and has a runbook; pages per shift are measured and capped Hundreds of alerts, most ignored, the important one lost among them Incident management A defined severity scale, an incident commander role that rotates, a communications role, a timeline kept live, and postmortem follow-through tracked as in Incident Response Whoever is loudest runs the bridge; the timeline is reconstructed from chat logs afterwards Capacity and performance Forecasts for the services that matter, load tests before known peaks, headroom policy Capacity is discovered when it runs out Production readiness A checklist a service passes before it takes traffic: SLO, on-call, runbook, dashboards, backup and restore tested, dependencies declared Services go live when the feature is done Toil reduction Measured hours of manual operational work per service, with a budget and a backlog to eliminate it The same restore run by hand every month by the same person Reliability investment case Incident cost and toil cost turned into the numbers in Reliability as an Economic Decision and Technical Debt Economics Reliability requests presented as engineering preference Reference Observability architecture that survives scale and cost Observability platforms are now one of the largest line items in many cloud bills, and the cost usually grows faster than the value because nobody decided what to collect. Decide the signals and their purpose first Logs for forensic detail, metrics for state over time and alerting, traces for request flow across services. A signal with no consumer is cost. Most estates over-collect logs and under-instrument traces. Standardize the instrumentation, not the vendor Use a vendor-neutral instrumentation standard (OpenTelemetry has become the default) so the collection layer is portable and the backend can be changed at a renewal. The backend is a SaaS renewal problem; the instrumentation should not be. Put a cost owner on telemetry Ingest volume by service, with a budget per service and an alert when it is exceeded. Sampling for traces, retention tiers for logs, cardinality limits for metrics. The observability bill is a FinOps problem and belongs in Cloud FinOps . Alert on symptoms, not causes Alerts derive from SLOs: error rate, latency, availability as the user sees them. Cause-level signals (CPU, disk, queue depth) feed dashboards and the investigation, not the pager. Make the correlation identifier non-negotiable One identifier propagates through every request, message, and log line. Without it, distributed debugging is guesswork, and the integration patterns in Integration & API Patterns depend on it. Include the AI layer Model calls, token usage, latency, cost, and output quality signals are telemetry too. An AI system in production without them is not observable; see AI Architecture . Reference On-call that people will keep doing The failure mode of every reliability model is an on-call rota that burns out the people who know the most. It is a design problem, not a resilience problem. Rotations are at least six people deep; fewer means someone is on call one week in four or worse On-call is paid, either as an allowance or as time off, and the policy is written down Pages per shift are measured; a shift with more than a handful of pages triggers a review of the alerts, not of the person Every page has a runbook; a page without one is a bug filed against the service, not a test of the responder Escalation is defined by service and by severity, with a named second line, so the first responder is never alone by default Follow-the-sun is used where the organization spans time zones; if it does not, night pages are minimized by design, not endured Toil discovered on call goes to a backlog with a budget, and the team sees it shrink New engineers shadow before they respond, and nobody is on the rota for a service they have never deployed Sequencing Standing the function up For an organization moving from an ops team to a reliability model, in the order that produces visible results without a reorganization. Step Move Evidence it is done 1 Define severity levels and an incident commander rotation; run the next three incidents that way Incident timelines exist; postmortems have owners and dates 2 Set SLOs for the five most important customer-facing services, measured from the user's side Five SLO dashboards; product owners can state their service's target 3 Cut the alert list to the ones tied to those SLOs; delete or demote the rest Pages per shift drop; every remaining page has a runbook 4 Publish a production readiness checklist and apply it to the next new service One service has gone live through the checklist; the gaps it revealed are in a backlog 5 Adopt a vendor-neutral instrumentation standard and a telemetry cost budget per service Ingest by service is visible; the observability bill is flat or falling as coverage rises 6 Write the error budget policy and get the CEO or CPO to sign it A feature release has been delayed once because a budget was exhausted, and the organization survived 7 Decide the operating model explicitly, fund it, and name what SRE owns versus what teams own An org design decision recorded in an ADR, with the on-call model and the funding that goes with it Common pitfall Renaming the ops team The most common SRE adoption is a change of job title. It produces a team with the same reactive workload, a new set of expectations, and no authority to change either. What it looks like The operations team becomes the SRE team. Product teams are told they are now on call, escalate every page to SRE within minutes, and ship services with no SLO and no runbook because the checklist has no teeth. SRE is paged for everything, owns nothing, and attrits. Leadership concludes that SRE does not work here. The counter-move The function owns standards and the platform, with a production readiness gate that product teams must pass and an error budget policy signed by the executive who owns the roadmap. Teams that meet the standard run their own services; the reliability function's success measure is how rarely it is paged for something it does not own. See Platform Engineering for the platform side of the same operating model and Org Design for where the function reports.

title: Regulatory Map for Technology Leaders
description: Which regulations reach a technology organization and when: GDPR, US state privacy laws, HIPAA, GLBA, NYDFS Part 500, SEC cyber disclosure, PCI DSS, CIRCIA, NIS2, DORA, the EU AI Act after the 2026 omnibus deferral, the Cyber Resilience Act, the Data Act, Colorado's AI Act, and UK regimes, with the clock and the owner for each, an applicability filter, and the one-process-per-regulation pitfall.
body: Regulatory Map for Technology Leaders Interactive Which regimes apply to us Tick what describes the organization. The list below narrows to the regimes most likely in scope, with the clock and the owner for each. This is a starting point for a conversation with counsel, not a determination. Runs in your browser; nothing is sent or stored. Show applicable regimes Show all Reference The regimes, by what they regulate Grouped by the thing they govern, because that is how ownership falls out. Dates are as enacted or as last amended; several are still moving and the caveat at the top applies to every row. Regime Who it reaches What it requires of technology The clock Status note GDPR (EU) and UK GDPR Anyone processing personal data of people in the EU or UK, wherever the organization sits Lawful basis, data minimization, records of processing, DPIAs, transfer mechanisms, subject rights made operational, security appropriate to risk Breach notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of awareness; to individuals without undue delay where high risk Stable. A separate EU digital omnibus proposing GDPR simplifications is in progress; verify before relying on it US state privacy laws (CCPA/CPRA and roughly twenty comprehensive state acts) Businesses meeting per-state revenue or volume thresholds with residents' data Rights requests, opt-outs, data inventories, contracts with processors, and in California automated decision-making technology rules Rights request response typically 45 days; breach notification per state breach statute, often 30 to 60 days New states add laws most years; California's ADMT regulations phase in through 2027. Track per state HIPAA (US) Covered entities and business associates handling protected health information Security Rule safeguards, risk analysis, BAAs with every vendor touching PHI, minimum necessary access Breach notification to individuals and HHS within 60 days of discovery; large breaches also to media A proposed Security Rule update (published January 2025) would make many addressable safeguards required, including MFA and encryption; check whether it has been finalized GLBA Safeguards Rule (US, FTC) Non-bank financial institutions: lenders, brokers, fintech, auto dealers, tax preparers A written security program, qualified individual, risk assessment, MFA, encryption, vendor oversight Notice to the FTC within 30 days of a breach affecting 500 or more consumers Stable since the 2024 notification amendment NYDFS Part 500 (New York) Entities licensed by the New York Department of Financial Services CISO, annual certification, MFA universally, asset inventory, privileged access controls, annual pen testing Notice within 72 hours of a cybersecurity incident; ransomware payment notice within 24 hours Amended 2023; phased requirements completed November 2025 SEC cybersecurity disclosure (US public companies) SEC registrants, including foreign private issuers A process for determining materiality without unreasonable delay; annual disclosure of risk management, strategy, and governance Form 8-K Item 1.05 within four business days of determining an incident is material Stable. The clock starts at the materiality determination, which is why the determination process itself must be designed PCI DSS (contractual, global) Anyone storing, processing, or transmitting cardholder data Twelve requirements; v4.0.1 future-dated requirements became mandatory March 2025 Assessed annually; incident notification per card brand and acquirer rules Not a law; a contract with the acquirer. Non-compliance costs fines and, eventually, the ability to take cards CIRCIA (US critical infrastructure) Covered entities across the sixteen critical infrastructure sectors, as defined by the final rule Incident reporting to CISA 72 hours from reasonable belief that a covered incident occurred; 24 hours after a ransom payment Enacted 2022; the final rule defining scope was still pending at last check, with CISA targeting late 2026. The clocks are in the statute and will not change; who they apply to is what the rule decides NIS2 (EU) Essential and important entities in eighteen sectors, plus their suppliers by contract; medium-sized and larger Risk management measures, supply chain security, management accountability with personal liability, incident handling Early warning within 24 hours; notification within 72 hours; final report within one month Transposition deadline was October 2024; member states transposed unevenly, so the applicable national law matters DORA (EU financial sector) Banks, insurers, investment firms, payment institutions, crypto-asset providers, and their critical ICT third-party providers ICT risk framework, incident classification and reporting, digital operational resilience testing including threat-led pen tests, a register of all ICT third-party arrangements, contractual requirements for providers Initial notification of a major ICT incident within 4 hours of classification and 24 hours of awareness; intermediate within 72 hours; final within one month Applied from January 2025. Critical third-party providers are designated by the European supervisory authorities EU AI Act Providers and deployers of AI systems placed on the EU market or affecting people in the EU Prohibited practices banned; general-purpose model obligations; transparency duties; for high-risk uses (employment, credit, education, biometrics, critical infrastructure, and others) risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight, conformity assessment Prohibitions applied February 2025; GPAI obligations August 2025; transparency duties August 2026; high-risk obligations for Annex III systems deferred to December 2027 and Annex I embedded systems to August 2028 by the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI The deferral was adopted mid-2026. The obligations did not go away; the deadline moved. The Commission retains the ability to bring the dates forward once standards are ready EU Cyber Resilience Act Manufacturers of products with digital elements sold in the EU, hardware and software, including SaaS components in some cases Secure-by-design requirements, vulnerability handling, SBOM, security updates for the support period, conformity assessment Reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents from September 2026; full obligations from December 2027 New; the reporting obligation lands before the product requirements, which surprises product teams EU Data Act Providers of connected products and related services, cloud and data processing services User access to product data, cloud switching and exit rights, egress fee phase-out, interoperability Applied from September 2025; contractual and switching provisions phase in Directly affects cloud contracts and exit clauses; see SaaS Contract & Renewal Negotiation Colorado AI Act (US) Developers and deployers of high-risk AI making consequential decisions about Colorado residents Risk management program, impact assessments, notices, and a duty of care against algorithmic discrimination, with NIST AI RMF or ISO 42001 alignment as an affirmative defense Effective date June 30, 2026 as amended Enforcement was stayed by a federal court in April 2026 pending litigation, and a legislative replacement was in progress. Treat as unsettled and watch the other states drafting from the same template UK NIS Regulations and Cyber Security and Resilience Bill UK operators of essential services, relevant digital service providers, and, under the bill, managed service providers and data centres Security duties, incident reporting, regulator oversight Incident reporting timelines set by each competent authority; the bill tightens to 24-hour initial notification The bill was introduced in 2025; check whether it has received Royal Assent and commenced Reference Voluntary frameworks that regulators and customers treat as the baseline None of these is law. All of them show up in customer questionnaires, regulator expectations, and affirmative defenses, which makes them the practical floor. Framework What it is for Where it carries weight NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 Organizing a security program across Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover US regulators and courts as a reasonableness standard; see Security & Compliance Maturity ISO/IEC 27001 A certifiable information security management system Enterprise procurement globally; often a contractual requirement SOC 2 Type II Attestation of controls over a period against the trust services criteria US enterprise procurement; says what was in scope, not what is true NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 Structuring AI risk management; 42001 is certifiable Affirmative defense under Colorado's act; expected evidence under the EU AI Act; see AI Governance CIS Controls A prioritized list of technical safeguards Cyber insurance underwriting and as a starting point for small programs Ownership Who owns which clock Regulatory failures are usually ownership failures. Every regime needs a named owner for the determination (does this apply, did this event trigger it), a named owner for the notification, and a named owner for the ongoing obligations. These are rarely the same person. Obligation type Typical owner What the CTO owns regardless Applicability determination General counsel, with the CISO and DPO Providing the accurate inventory of systems, data, locations, and AI uses that the determination depends on Incident and breach notification CISO for the clock; counsel for the content; CEO or CFO for SEC materiality The detection capability that starts the clock honestly, and the timeline of what happened, in minutes, not adjectives. See Incident Response Privacy rights and data handling DPO or privacy officer The ability to find, export, and delete a person's data across the estate, which is an architecture problem. See Data Governance & Privacy Operational resilience and testing CTO or CIO, with the CISO DR testing evidence, RTO and RPO, and threat-led testing under DORA. See Disaster Recovery Third-party and supply chain Procurement with the CISO The register of ICT providers, the contractual terms on security and exit, and concentration risk AI system obligations Whoever owns the AI portfolio, usually the CTO or CDO Classification of every AI use against the high-risk categories, logging, human oversight, and the technical documentation Board reporting on all of the above CISO and CTO, jointly One consolidated view of which regimes apply, the open obligations, and the incidents notified. See Board Reporting Common pitfall Building one process per regulation Organizations that treat each regime as its own project end up with six incident procedures, four data inventories, and no idea which one is current. What it looks like The GDPR breach process lives with the DPO, the SEC materiality process with the general counsel, the NYDFS notification with the compliance team, and the HIPAA process with the privacy officer. An incident occurs. Four teams run four assessments in parallel with four timelines, none of them share a fact base, and the 72-hour clock expires while the materiality committee is being scheduled. The counter-move One incident process with one fact base and one timeline, with a regulatory overlay that maps the facts to each applicable clock. One control library mapped to every framework once, as in Governance, Risk & Compliance . One data inventory serving privacy, security, AI classification, and diligence. The regimes differ in their thresholds and their clocks, not in what they need to know.

title: M&A Diligence Kit: Question Bank, Data Room, Sell-Side Prep
description: A prioritized technology diligence question bank across architecture, security, data, operations, people, IP, and cost, with what a bad answer looks like; a four-tier data room structure; and a six-month sell-side preparation sequence for technology leaders on the selling side of a transaction.
body: M&A Diligence Kit: Question Bank, Data Room, Sell-Side Prep How to use Three tools, two sides of the table The question bank is what a buyer asks. The data room structure is how a seller answers before being asked. The sell-side guide is what a technology leader does in the months before a process starts so that the answers exist. Read the one for your side, then the other one, because the counterparty will. Tool Buy-side use Sell-side use Question bank The interview and document-request list, prioritized so a two-week confirmatory window covers what moves price first The list to answer internally, honestly, six months before a buyer asks, so nothing in it is a surprise Data room template What to request if the seller's room is disorganized, and a checklist of what is missing The folder structure to populate, with the four-tier access model that protects what should not be shown until late Sell-side preparation The signals that a target prepared well, which correlates with fewer post-close surprises The sequence of work from the decision to sell through the first buyer meeting Question bank Architecture and technical debt Priority 1 questions should be answered before a price is agreed. Priority 2 belong in confirmatory diligence. Priority 3 inform the integration plan. Priority Question Ask via What a bad answer looks like 1 Draw the system as it runs today, not the target architecture, and mark what fewer than three people understand Interview A slide from the last investor deck; nobody in the room can draw the current state 1 Which runtimes, databases, and frameworks are past vendor end of life, and what is the plan and cost to move Doc A list has to be compiled for the question; extended support contracts nobody mentioned 1 What is the technical debt backlog, with a cost of remediation and a carry cost per item Doc A backlog of tickets with no costs, or a statement that debt is under control with no artifact 1 How is the platform hosted, in which regions and accounts, and who holds the root credentials Doc A shared root account, a personal credit card on a cloud account, production in a region the buyer cannot operate in 2 What is the deployment frequency, change failure rate, and time to restore for the core product over the last twelve months Doc Numbers unavailable; deployments happen monthly by one person on a weekend 2 What third-party components, open-source licenses, and embedded SDKs are in the product, and which carry copyleft or commercial obligations Doc No software bill of materials; a GPL dependency in a commercially licensed product 2 Which parts of the product would have to be rewritten to scale ten times, and has anyone estimated it Interview Everyone agrees it will scale; the load test is from three years ago 3 What does a full environment rebuild from source and backups take, and when was it last done Interview Never; the environment was built by hand and the person who built it left Question bank Security, compliance, and data Certifications tell you what was in scope for an audit. These questions tell you what is true. Priority Question Ask via What a bad answer looks like 1 Which systems and products are in scope for each certification held, and which revenue-bearing systems are out of scope Doc The SOC 2 covers the corporate network and not the product that drives the valuation 1 List every security incident, breach, or near-miss in the last three years, with notifications made and outcomes Doc None reported, and a customer contract on file references a credit for a breach 1 Where is customer and employee personal data stored and processed, under which legal entity and jurisdiction, and what lawful basis and transfer mechanism applies Doc Data in three clouds across two continents with no record of why; sub-processors not listed 1 How many accounts hold privileged access across the cloud tenants and directory, and how many of those have phishing-resistant MFA and time-bound elevation Doc Twelve permanent global admins, two belonging to former employees; see Identity & Access Architecture 2 When was the last external penetration test, what were the critical and high findings, and which are still open Doc Test is two years old; criticals open with no date 2 What data does the product send to AI or ML providers, under which terms, and with what retention Doc Customer data sent to a consumer AI tool by the support team under default terms 2 Which customer contracts carry security, availability, or data-residency commitments that exceed what the platform delivers Doc A 99.99 percent SLA on a platform with no redundancy; residency promised in a region not used 3 What is the backup, restore, and disaster recovery posture, and when was a restore last tested end to end Interview Backups exist; restore never tested; RTO and RPO undefined Question bank Operations, organization, IP, and cost The questions that most often reprice a deal are here, and they are the ones diligence teams under time pressure skip. Priority Question Ask via What a bad answer looks like 1 For each system that generates revenue, name the people who can change it in production, and their tenure, compensation, and retention terms Doc One name repeated across every system; no retention agreements; that person has not been told about the deal 1 Who owns the intellectual property in the product: employee and contractor assignment agreements, open-source contributions, university or prior-employer claims Doc Contractors with no assignment clause built the core; a founder's prior employer has a plausible claim 1 What is the fully loaded run cost of the platform by month for the last 24 months, and what drives the variance Doc Cloud bill grew 60 percent with no revenue growth to match; reserved commitments expire at close 1 Which contracts have change-of-control, assignment, or most-favored-customer clauses, and which vendors gain leverage at close Doc The core database vendor's license terminates on change of control 2 What is the engineering headcount by role, level, location, and employment type, and what is regretted attrition over 24 months Doc Half the team are contractors through one agency; attrition unmeasured 2 What does the on-call rota look like, how many incidents per month, and what is the escalation path when the first responder cannot fix it Interview Two people on permanent call; escalation is the CTO's mobile 2 Which product commitments have been made to customers or the market that are not yet built, and what would they cost Interview A roadmap sold to enterprise customers that engineering has not seen 3 What tooling, licenses, and subscriptions exist, who owns each, and which would the combined entity duplicate Doc No inventory; several tools paid by individuals on expense 3 For healthcare or financial targets specifically: which regulatory registrations, business associate agreements, and audit obligations transfer, and which must be re-executed Doc BAAs with the wrong entity; a state licensure requirement nobody on the deal team knows about Template Data room structure with a four-tier access model A well-organized technology data room signals a well-run technology function. The tiers control what a buyer sees at each stage, so that the most sensitive material is only visible to a buyer who has earned it. Tier Who sees it When Folders 1: Overview Any qualified buyer under NDA Teaser and first management meeting 01 Technology overview narrative; 02 Architecture summary (current state, one page); 03 Team structure and headcount summary; 04 Certifications and attestations held; 05 Product roadmap summary 2: Confirmatory Buyers who have submitted an indicative offer Confirmatory diligence 06 Detailed architecture and data flow diagrams; 07 Technical debt register with costs; 08 Engineering metrics, 24 months; 09 Security policies, last pen test summary, incident register; 10 Data inventory and privacy documentation; 11 Third-party components and license inventory; 12 Infrastructure and run cost, 24 months; 13 Vendor contract summaries with change-of-control flags 3: Restricted Final bidder or bidders, named individuals only Exclusivity 14 Full pen test reports and open findings; 15 Employee and contractor agreements, IP assignments; 16 Key-person list with compensation and retention terms; 17 Customer contract exceptions (SLA, residency, security commitments); 18 Open litigation, regulatory correspondence, and audit findings 4: Clean team Outside counsel and designated clean-team members only Post-exclusivity, pre-close 19 Source code access (read-only, escrowed, or on-site review); 20 Production access evidence (privileged account export); 21 Customer-identifiable data, where its review is legally necessary Every folder has an index file naming its contents and its owner. Every document is dated. Nothing is uploaded that the technology leader has not read; a data room is a set of representations, and the buyer's counsel will treat it as one. Sell-side preparation The six months before a process Most sell-side technology preparation is a scramble after the banker's request list arrives. The work below, done early, changes the price and shortens the process. Month 6: Answer the question bank internally Run every priority 1 and 2 question above against your own organization, in writing, as if you were the buyer. The gaps are the preparation plan. This is a Technology Diligence exercise pointed at yourself. Month 5: Fix what is cheap and visible Remove former employees' access. Eliminate standing privileged access. Close open critical pen test findings. Retire the end-of-life version that would appear in every buyer's report. These cost weeks and remove findings that cost millions in price. Month 4: Build the artifacts that do not exist A current-state architecture diagram. A technical debt register with costs, using Technical Debt Economics . A software bill of materials. An inventory of privileged accounts and non-human identities. A run-cost history with variance explained. A buyer will produce these if you do not, and theirs will be less flattering. Month 3: Paper the people and the IP IP assignment agreements for every current and former contributor. Retention agreements for the named key people, executed before they hear about the process from anyone else. A succession answer for each critical system, using CTO Leadership & Succession . Month 2: Review the contracts Every customer contract for SLA, residency, and security commitments the platform does not meet; every vendor contract for change-of-control and assignment clauses. Renegotiate or document the exposure. Do not let the buyer find it. Month 1: Build the data room and rehearse the narrative Populate tiers 1 and 2. Write the technology overview narrative as prose, not slides, describing the estate as it is, with its known weaknesses and their remediation plan stated plainly. A buyer who finds a weakness you disclosed treats you as credible; one who finds a weakness you omitted reprices everything. Common pitfall Disclosing the target state instead of the current state The most common sell-side failure is presenting the architecture the team is building toward as if it were the architecture that exists. What it looks like The overview shows microservices, event streaming, and a zero-trust network. The buyer's engineers find a monolith, a nightly batch, and a flat network with the target-state work six months from done. Every other representation in the data room is now suspect, the confirmatory window extends, and the price moves. The counter-move Show the current state, honestly labeled, alongside the target state, honestly dated and costed. Buyers expect debt; what they price is surprise. A credible current-state picture with a funded plan is worth more than an aspirational one, and it is the only version that survives the buyer's own engineers reading the code.

title: SaaS Contract & Renewal Negotiation
description: Where SaaS money is actually lost (auto-renewal uplifts, shelfware, tier creep, uncapped consumption), the renewal calendar as a control with a 180-day sequence, the contract clauses that decide the next renewal, how to run the renewal conversation against a vendor's sales playbook, a worked $400k example, and the procurement-owns-the-paper pitfall.
body: SaaS Contract & Renewal Negotiation Framework Where the money is actually lost Selection gets the attention. Renewal is where most of the money goes, because the vendor knows the switching cost, the contract auto-renews at an uplift, and the person who negotiated the original deal has usually moved on. Leak How it happens Typical size Auto-renewal at list uplift The contract renews for another term with a 5 to 10 percent increase unless notice is given 60 to 90 days before the end date, and nobody owns the calendar The uplift compounds every year; over a five-year relationship the price can be 40 percent above the original Shelfware Licenses bought for a planned headcount or a rollout that never reached full adoption, renewed at the same count because nobody checked utilization Commonly 20 to 35 percent of seats in enterprise SaaS estates; higher in tools bought during growth Tier creep A feature needed by one team moves the whole organization to the next tier The tier delta multiplied by every seat Consumption without a cap Usage-based pricing (API calls, tokens, compute, data volume) with no committed level and no alert Unpredictable; the first sign is the invoice Duplicate tools Two teams bought two products that do the same thing, each below the approval threshold The smaller of the two contracts, plus the integration cost of both Renewal timing under pressure The renewal lands during a quarter-end crunch or a leadership change and is signed to make it go away Whatever leverage existed, forfeited Reference The renewal calendar as a control The single highest-return artifact in vendor management is a calendar. It is also the one most organizations do not have. For every contract above a threshold (set it low; $25k a year catches most of the leaks), record: the end date, the notice deadline, the auto-renewal terms, the current annual value, the uplift clause, the utilization, and the named owner. Review it monthly. Anything with a notice deadline inside 180 days gets a negotiation plan; anything inside 90 days without one is already late. The 180-day mark matters because it is roughly when a credible alternative can still be evaluated. Once the vendor knows you cannot switch before the renewal date, the negotiation is about their willingness to be reasonable, and the calendar was the thing that could have given you leverage. Days before end date Action 180 Pull utilization. Decide whether this is a renew, renegotiate, downsize, consolidate, or exit. If renegotiate or exit, name the alternative and start evaluating it, visibly. 120 Send the vendor a written notice of intent to renegotiate, with the specific asks. Ask for the price of the alternative in writing. Involve procurement. 90 Serve any contractual non-renewal notice required to preserve the option, even if you expect to renew. A served notice can be withdrawn; a missed one cannot. 60 Final terms agreed or the exit plan in motion. Anything still open here is being negotiated under time pressure, which is the vendor's preferred condition. 0 Signed terms filed in one place, calendar updated with the new dates, utilization baseline reset. Reference The clauses that decide the next renewal The negotiation that matters most happens at the first signing, because that is when the renewal terms are set. These are the clauses to fix then, and to fix retroactively at the next renewal if they were missed. Clause Ask for Why Renewal uplift A cap (ideally zero to 3 percent, or tied to a published index), applying to all renewals, not just the first An uncapped uplift is a blank cheque; a cap on the first renewal only moves the problem one year Auto-renewal and notice No auto-renewal, or a notice period of 30 days or less, and the vendor's obligation to notify you 90 days before the deadline Puts the burden of the calendar on the side that benefits from you missing it Seat flexibility The right to reduce seat count at renewal, and true-down at least annually for consumption Otherwise every optimistic forecast becomes a permanent floor Price hold and most-favored terms Pricing held for the full term, and a commitment that new customers of similar size are not offered materially better terms Prevents the list price from being renegotiated in the middle of a term through a product repackaging Tier and packaging protection Features you have today stay in your tier for the term; repackaging cannot force an upgrade Repackaging is the most common way SaaS vendors raise effective prices without touching the rate card Data exit Full export in a documented, non-proprietary format, at no charge, within 30 days of termination, with the data retained for that period Without this the switching cost is whatever the vendor decides it is. In the EU, the Data Act now supports switching rights for cloud services; use it Termination for convenience or for cause A clear right to terminate for material breach including SLA failure, and where possible for convenience with a notice period A contract that can only end at the renewal date has one negotiation point per term Security and compliance Right to audit or to receive current attestations, breach notification within a defined window, sub-processor change notice, and the ability to object See Regulatory Map for the regimes that make this mandatory rather than optional Assignment and change of control The contract survives your own change of control and the vendor's, at the same terms Otherwise an acquisition on either side reopens the price; see M&A Diligence Kit Service levels with teeth Credits that are meaningful, an escalation path, and termination rights after repeated failure A 99.9 percent SLA with a 5 percent credit is a marketing statement Method Running the renewal conversation Vendors run renewals as a sales process with a playbook, a quota, and a quarter-end. Most customers run them as an admin task. The asymmetry is the whole problem. Know your number before theirs Utilization, value realized, the cost of the alternative including migration, and the internal budget. If you cannot say what the product is worth to you, the vendor will say it for you. Make the alternative real A credible evaluation of a competitor, or of doing without, changes the vendor's behavior more than any argument. It does not have to be a bluff to work; it has to be visible. Use the vendor's calendar Vendors discount at their quarter-end and year-end. If your renewal date does not align, ask to move it. A three-month extension to reach their fiscal year-end is often worth more than any other single lever. Trade term for price, carefully A longer commitment is the vendor's favorite ask. Accept it only with the uplift cap, the seat flexibility, and the exit terms above, so that a three-year deal does not become three years of leverage for them. Bundle the asks Bring the clause corrections, the price, and any service issues to the same conversation. Vendors will fix contract terms in exchange for a renewal they were worried about; they will not reopen the contract mid-term. Escalate above the account executive The AE's discount authority is limited and their incentive is to close at the highest price that does not lose the deal. A conversation between your executive and theirs, at the right moment, changes both. Get everything in the order form Verbal commitments about roadmap, support, or future pricing are worth nothing at the next renewal. If it matters, it is in the signed document. Worked example A $400k renewal The pattern recurs at every scale. Without the calendar The contract for a collaboration platform, $400k a year, 2,000 seats, auto-renews at 8 percent with 90 days' notice. Nobody notices until the invoice arrives at $432k. Utilization was 1,300 seats. The vendor points to the notice clause. The organization pays $432k for a year, of which roughly $150k is for seats nobody uses, and is now negotiating the following year from the same position. With it At 180 days, utilization shows 1,300 active seats. A competitor evaluation begins, visibly. At 120 days the vendor is told the intent is to renew at 1,400 seats, flat price per seat, with an uplift cap and true-down rights, or to migrate. At 90 days non-renewal notice is served to preserve the option. The vendor, facing a quarter-end and a live competitor, agrees to 1,400 seats at a 5 percent per-seat discount, 3 percent cap, annual true-down. The renewal lands at $266k. The difference funds two engineers. Common pitfall Procurement owns the contract, nobody owns the value Handing renewals to procurement produces better paper and the same shelfware, because procurement can negotiate the rate but not the seat count, the tier, or whether the product is needed at all. What it looks like Procurement negotiates a 7 percent discount on a renewal for a tool the engineering team stopped using six months ago. The discount is reported as a saving. The tool is renewed for two more years. The counter-move Every contract has a business owner who answers three questions at 180 days: are we using it, do we still need it, and what is it worth. Procurement then negotiates the terms for the answer. Tie the owner's answer to the utilization data, not to their preference, and make the total contract value by owner visible in the technology budget so that shelfware has a name attached to it.
